summary: Describes using the SEED block cipher in Cipher Block Chaining mode, with an explicit IV, for confidentiality in IPsec ESP. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec scrambles internet messages so only the right people can read them. This memo adds a new scrambler, called SEED, to its toolbox.

questions: how does cbc mode work in ipsec
subtitle: How to encrypt IPsec ESP traffic with the SEED block cipher in CBC mode with a fresh random IV in every packet.

tldr.problem: IPsec ESP needs a choice of encryption algorithms, and SEED, a 128-bit block cipher widely used in South Korea, had no defined way to be used with it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies SEED in CBC mode: a 16-octet random IV is placed at the front of each ESP payload, the data is padded to a multiple of 16 octets, and IKE uses transform identifier 21 for ESP_SEED_CBC.
tldr.outcome: It supplies the rules, identifiers and six test cases needed to interoperate. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 4196 is a Proposed Standard from October 2005. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The SEED Cipher and Its Role
sections.content:
SEED is a national industrial association standard that the RFC says is widely used in South Korea for electronic commerce and financial services. It is a 128-bit symmetric key block cipher developed by KISA (Korea Information Security Agency) and a group of experts since 1998. Block size and key length are both 128 bits.

The cipher has a 16-round Feistel structure. The 128-bit input is split into two 64-bit halves, and the right half goes into the round function with a 64-bit subkey produced by key scheduling. The RFC states that SEED resists differential and linear cryptanalysis and related key attacks, and that ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27 and Japan's CRYPTREC evaluated it as secure.

This document only describes how to use SEED inside the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). The cipher itself is specified elsewhere, in RFC 4009.
sections.plainLanguage: SEED is a secret-code machine that scrambles messages in chunks of the same size. This memo explains how to plug it into IPsec's mail system.

sections.title: CBC Mode, Keys, Padding
sections.content:
The RFC picks CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) from the NIST modes because it is well understood and currently required for all other ESP ciphers. CBC needs an Initialization Vector (IV) the same size as the block. The IV is XORed with the first plaintext block before encryption, and after that each ciphertext block is XORed with the next plaintext block. A random IV stops identical data in different packets from producing identical ciphertext.

The key is 128 bits and there are 16 rounds. At the time of writing there were no known weak keys for SEED.

The block size is 16 octets. Padding MUST be added, as RFC 2406 specifies, so that the data to encrypt (including the ESP Pad Length and Next Header fields) is a multiple of 16 octets. That also keeps those two fields right-aligned in a 4-octet word, so no extra alignment padding is needed. More padding MAY be added if the 16-octet block size is kept.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk is mixed with the scrambled chunk before it, like links in a chain, so repeats do not look the same. If a message does not fill the last chunk, it is padded to fit.

sections.title: The ESP Payload with a Random IV
sections.content:
The ESP payload is a 16-octet IV followed by the encrypted payload, whose length is a multiple of 16 octets. The IV is the same size as the cipher's block size.

The IV MUST be chosen at random and MUST be unpredictable. Implementations MUST NOT use a counter or another low-Hamming-distance source for IVs, so that very similar plaintext blocks in different packets are not encrypted in a similar way.

Because each datagram carries its own IV, every received datagram can be decrypted even when other datagrams are dropped or reordered in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet carries its own starting number for the scrambler, picked at random. So even if some packets get lost or shuffled, each can still be unscrambled on its own.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
Six test cases let implementers check their work. The first two test SEED-CBC encryption alone: Case 1 encrypts 32 bytes (2 blocks) and Case 2 encrypts 64 bytes (4 blocks), each with a 128-bit key. Each lists the key, the IV, the plaintext and the resulting ciphertext in hexadecimal.

The last four show sample ESP packets. Cases 3 and 4 are transport mode, using a ping to 192.168.123.100 with SPI 4321. Cases 5 and 6 are tunnel mode, using a ping to 192.168.123.200 with SPI 8765 and the next header 04 (IP-in-IP). For each, the RFC shows the original packet, the padding, pad length and next header added, the data before encryption, and the final packet with SPI, sequence number, IV and encrypted data.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo includes worked answers, so anyone building SEED can check that their scrambler gives the same result as everyone else's.

sections.title: Negotiating SEED with IKE
sections.content:
IKE sets up the ESP security associations that use SEED-CBC. In Phase 1 the algorithm is identified by the object identifier id-seedCBC, defined in RFC 4009. In Phase 2 IANA has assigned the ESP Transform Identifier 21 to ESP_SEED_CBC.

Since SEED has only a 128-bit key, the Key Length attribute is set to 128 bits. HMAC-SHA-1 and HMAC-MD5 are considered strong enough both to generate 128-bit SEED keys in IKE and to authenticate ESP packets protected by SEED.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two computers talk secretly, they agree which scrambler to use. SEED has its own agreed name and number, and its key is always the same size.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that no security problem has been found on SEED and that it is secure against all known attacks, including differential and linear cryptanalysis and related key attacks. The best known attack is an exhaustive search for the key, according to the CRYPTREC evaluation. Readers are pointed to CRYPTREC, the ISO report and KISA's self-evaluation for more.

These are the document's own claims as of 2005. For use in ESP, the IV rules above (random, unpredictable, no counters) are the main protections the RFC itself requires.
sections.plainLanguage: As of this memo, nobody had found a shortcut for breaking SEED, other than trying every key.
